---
title: "Recovering the EZ diffusion model on the standard grid"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
options(width = 90)
# paths relative to the package root, whether this renders from the
# package root (pkgdown) or from vignettes/articles
from_root <- function(path) {
  if (dir.exists("vignettes")) path else file.path("..", "..", path)
}
# the code shown is read from the script that produced the results
shown <- function(label, file) {
  lines <- readLines(from_root(file))
  markers <- grep("^## ---- ", lines)
  start <- markers[lines[markers] == paste("## ----", label)]
  end <- c(markers[markers > start], length(lines) + 1L)[[1L]] - 1L
  code <- lines[(start + 1L):end]
  while (length(code) > 0L && !nzchar(trimws(code[[length(code)]]))) {
    code <- code[-length(code)]
  }
  code
}
script <- "vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R"
script_url <- paste0(
  "https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/blob/main/", script
)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
library(bmmtools)
```

```{r data, include = FALSE}
res <- readRDS(from_root("vignettes/articles/assets/recovery-ezdm.rds"))
out <- res$out
bmm_version <- res$toolchain[["bmm"]]
reps <- length(unique(res$cells$replication))
cells <- res$cells
pop <- res$population
sds <- res$families$sd
subj <- res$families$subject
rel <- res$reliability
rel <- rel[match(
  paste(subj$condition, subj$term), paste(rel$condition, rel$term)
), ]
cors <- res$correlations
readoff <- res$readoff
rows <- as.data.frame(out)
# one row of a table, by design and term; anything but exactly one row is
# an error, so a regenerated asset cannot silently shift the prose
pick <- function(x, n, t, term = NULL) {
  keep <- x$n_subjects == n & x$n_trials == t
  if (!is.null(term)) keep <- keep & x$term == term
  out <- x[keep, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1L)
  out
}
smallest <- function(n, threshold, column = "smallest_with_coverage") {
  out <- readoff[readoff$n_subjects == n & readoff$threshold == threshold, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1L)
  out[[column]]
}
# the condition label of one design, for the per-design scatter plots
design_of <- function(n, t) {
  d <- res$design[res$design$n_subjects == n & res$design$n_trials == t, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d$condition
}
# a 95 % Wilson score interval for k of n, as plot_design() draws it
wilson <- function(k, n, z = stats::qnorm(0.975)) {
  p <- k / n
  centre <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  spread <- z / (1 + z^2 / n) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2))
  c(centre - spread, centre + spread)
}
interval <- function(k, n) paste(fmt(wilson(k, n)), collapse = " to ")
covered <- function(p) paste0(round(p * reps), "/", reps)
with_mcse <- function(x, se) paste0(fmt(x), " ± ", fmt(se, 3))
pars <- res$pars
accuracy <- stats::plogis(pars[["drift"]] * exp(pars[["bound"]]))
mean_rt <- exp(pars[["ndt"]]) + exp(pars[["bound"]]) /
  (2 * pars[["drift"]]) * tanh(pars[["drift"]] * exp(pars[["bound"]]) / 2)
# convergence: which fits fail the gate, and on which parameter the
# lowest bulk ESS of each sits (recorded by the precompute from the fits)
n_pass <- sum(cells$converged)
n_pass_101 <- sum(cells$converged_101)
failing <- cells[!cells$converged, ]
n_fail <- nrow(failing)
n_fail_30 <- sum(failing$n_trials == 30)
fail_on_cor <- sum(grepl("^cor_", failing$min_ess_bulk_parameter))
# coverage pooled over every design, per level and term: does the Wilson
# interval of the 95 % and of the 50 % intervals contain the nominal rate?
pooled <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(rows[rows$level %in% c("population", "sd"), ], ~ level + term,
    drop = TRUE
  ),
  function(d) {
    contains <- function(k, nominal) {
      w <- wilson(k, nrow(d))
      w[[1]] <= nominal && nominal <= w[[2]]
    }
    data.frame(
      level = d$level[[1]], term = d$term[[1]],
      nominal_95 = contains(sum(d$covered), 0.95),
      nominal_50 = contains(sum(d$covered_50), 0.5)
    )
  }
))
pop_ndt <- pooled$level == "population" & pooled$term == "ndt"
pop_rows <- rows[rows$level == "population", ]
ndt_rows <- pop_rows[pop_rows$term == "ndt", ]
ndt_50 <- sum(ndt_rows$covered_50)
ndt_95 <- sum(ndt_rows$covered)
# 20 against 50 subjects, matched on trials and term
paired <- function(x, column) {
  a <- x[x$n_subjects == 20, ]
  b <- x[x$n_subjects == 50, ]
  b <- b[match(paste(a$n_trials, a$term), paste(b$n_trials, b$term)), ]
  data.frame(term = a$term, at_20 = a[[column]], at_50 = b[[column]])
}
width <- paired(pop, "ci_width")
rmse <- paired(pop, "rmse")
r_pair <- paired(subj, "r")
# the bound coverage of 50 subjects at 30 and 100 trials, as a count
bound_k <- round(pick(pop, 50, 30, "bound")$coverage * reps)
# the SD row with the largest bias, and the SD rows lowest at 300 trials
sd_worst <- sds[which.max(abs(sds$bias)), ]
sd_300 <- sds[sds$n_trials == 300, ]
sd_low <- sd_300[sd_300$coverage == min(sd_300$coverage), ]
sd_low <- sd_low[order(sd_low$term, sd_low$n_subjects), ]
# how far the converged-only summary moves r_low
conv_subj <- res$families_converged$subject
r_low_shift <- max(abs(
  conv_subj$r_low[match(
    paste(subj$condition, subj$term),
    paste(conv_subj$condition, conv_subj$term)
  )] - subj$r_low
))
# the generating correlation of 0.4, and the in-sample correlations
cor_rows <- as.data.frame(attr(out, "correlations"))
in_sample <- tapply(
  cor_rows$sample_value, paste(cor_rows$condition, cor_rows$term), mean
)
cors$in_sample <- in_sample[paste(cors$condition, cors$term)]
target <- cors[cors$true_value == 0.4, ]
# posterior SD over prior SD at the smallest contraction
sd_ratio <- sqrt(1 - min(pop$contraction, na.rm = TRUE))
readoff <- readoff[order(readoff$n_subjects, readoff$threshold), ]
pair_label <- c(
  bound__drift = "drift – bound", bound__ndt = "bound – ndt",
  drift__ndt = "drift – ndt"
)
# the figures summarise `out` with the installed bmmtools; the tables
# read what the precompute stored. They must agree.
live <- summary(out)
agrees <- function(stored, columns, level) {
  l <- as.data.frame(live)[live$level == level, ]
  l <- l[match(
    paste(stored$condition, stored$term), paste(l$condition, l$term)
  ), ]
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    as.matrix(l[columns]), as.matrix(stored[columns]),
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
}
# the read-off by hand, and as smallest_design() gives it: the largest
# answer over the terms, per number of subjects
by_package <- function(threshold, coverage_check) {
  d <- smallest_design(
    live[live$level %in% c("subject", "population"), ],
    c(r_low = threshold),
    coverage_check = coverage_check
  )
  vapply(split(d$smallest, d$n_subjects), function(v) {
    if (anyNA(v)) NA_real_ else max(v)
  }, numeric(1))
}
same_answer <- function(column, coverage_check) {
  all(vapply(c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9), function(t) {
    hand <- readoff[readoff$threshold == t, ]
    pkg <- by_package(t, coverage_check)[as.character(hand$n_subjects)]
    identical(unname(pkg), as.numeric(hand[[column]]))
  }, logical(1)))
}
# the prose below states these; a regenerated asset must still satisfy them
stopifnot(
  reps == 10,
  smallest(50, 0.8) == 300, smallest(50, 0.7) == 300,
  smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest") == 100, smallest(20, 0.7) == 100,
  is.na(smallest(50, 0.9)), smallest(20, 0.8) == 300,
  smallest(20, 0.8, "smallest_point") == 100,
  same_answer("smallest_with_coverage", TRUE),
  same_answer("smallest", FALSE),
  pick(pop, 50, 30, "bound")$coverage == 0.8,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage == 0.8,
  pick(pop, 50, 300, "bound")$coverage == 0.9,
  !pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage_ok,
  all(pop$coverage_ok[pop$n_trials == 300]),
  all(abs(pop$bias) < 0.05),
  all(subj$r[subj$term == "drift"] < subj$r[subj$term == "bound"]),
  pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low < 0.8,
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low >= 0.8,
  all(cells$status == "ok"),
  all(target$coverage >= 0.9),
  n_fail_30 > n_fail / 2, fail_on_cor > n_fail / 2,
  all(grepl("^(cor|sd)_", failing$min_ess_bulk_parameter)),
  ndt_95 == nrow(ndt_rows), !pooled$nominal_50[pop_ndt],
  all(pooled$nominal_95[!pop_ndt] & pooled$nominal_50[!pop_ndt]),
  all(width$at_20 > width$at_50),
  all(rmse$at_20[rmse$term == "drift"] > rmse$at_50[rmse$term == "drift"]),
  max(abs(r_pair$at_20 - r_pair$at_50)) < 0.05,
  pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage * reps == bound_k,
  wilson(bound_k, reps)[[2]] < 0.95, wilson(bound_k, reps)[[2]] > 0.9,
  sd_worst$term == "drift", all(abs(subj$coverage - 0.95) < 0.05),
  pick(target, 50, 300)$rejection_rate ==
    max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 50]),
  pick(target, 20, 300)$rejection_rate ==
    max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 20]),
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r >= 0.9,
  pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low < 0.9,
  agrees(pop, c("bias", "rmse", "coverage", "ci_width"), "population"),
  agrees(sds, c("bias", "rmse", "coverage", "ci_width"), "sd"),
  agrees(subj, c("r", "r_low", "r_high"), "subject"),
  agrees(rel, "reliability_model", "subject")
)
```

This page reports one parameter recovery study of the three-parameter
EZ diffusion model, `bmm::ezdm()`, fitted with bmm `r bmm_version`. The
model describes each person's accuracy and response times by a drift
rate (`drift`), a boundary separation (`bound`) and a non-decision time
(`ndt`), estimated in one Bayesian hierarchical model. Data were
simulated from known parameter values, the model was fitted to
them, and the estimates were compared with the values that generated
the data. A researcher planning an EZ diffusion study can read from it
how well each parameter is recovered with 20 or 50 subjects and 30, 100
or 300 trials per subject, and how many trials per person an analysis of
individual differences needs. It does not say how many subjects a study
of group means or of correlations between parameters needs; it shows
only what 20 and 50 subjects give.

A *design* is one combination of subjects and trials; the grid has six.
Each design was simulated and fitted `r reps` times, the
*replications*, so the study has `r nrow(cells)` fits. The page reads
every number from the stored results of those fits, so the page builds
without refitting anything. bmmtools plans a *validation card* for each
model it supports, a standard report on the same grid of designs; the
card for `ezdm` will replace this page
([issue #21](https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmmtools/issues/21)).

**Reading the figures.** Most figures below are drawn by
`plot_design()`: a quantity on the y axis, the number of trials on a log
x axis, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects, and one panel per
parameter. Each panel has its own y axis. A point is the mean over a
design's ten replications, and its bar shows how precisely ten
replications pin that mean down. For bias, RMSE and interval width the
bar is ±1 *Monte Carlo standard error* (MCSE), the SD over the
replications divided by √10. For coverage and other shares the bar is a
95 % *Wilson interval*: the range of true shares that the observed count
is consistent with. It stays between 0 and 1 and is not empty at 10 of
10: ten covered intervals out of ten are consistent with a true coverage
as low as `r fmt(wilson(10, 10)[[1]])`, the lower end of the bar. A
dashed line marks the target where there is one: zero for bias, the
nominal 0.95 for coverage. The help page of `plot_design()` states the
source of every bar. The numbers behind each figure are in a table under
it, folded away; the text does not need them.

## The model and the generating values

The values below are on each parameter's link scale, explained after
the code.

```{r model, eval = FALSE, code = shown("model", script)}
```

Each parameter is estimated on its *link scale*, the unbounded scale
the model works on: `drift` as it is, `bound` and `ndt` as logarithms,
so a between-subject SD of 0.2 on `ndt` means people differ by about
20 % in non-decision time. The three-parameter EZ model fixes `s`, the
within-trial noise of the diffusion process, to 1. At these population
values a person answers correctly on `r fmt(100 * accuracy, 1)` % of
trials, with a mean response time of `r fmt(mean_rt, 2)` s (the
EZ expressions for accuracy and mean response time with `s = 1`).
`prior_sd` holds the prior SD of each parameter under bmm's default
priors; it is used for the *contraction* reported in the tables.

## The run

```{r run, eval = FALSE, code = shown("run", script)}
```

`reps = 10` is the number of replications per design. bmmtools
`r res$run_info$bmmtools_version`, which ran the script, did not pass
`seed` on to the chains' starting values, so a second run gave estimates
that differ in the third decimal; later versions seed them too. The one
place where that matters is said below.

<details>
<summary>What the other arguments do</summary>

`re_cor = "all"` lets the model estimate all three between-subject
correlations. `levels` and `correlations = "model"` choose what is
compared with the truth: the population means, the between-subject SDs,
every subject's parameters, and the model's correlation estimates.
`seed` fixes the simulated data and the sampler's seed. The arguments
after it go to `bmm::bmm()`: four chains of 2000 iterations each, the
first 1000 of them warm-up. The help page of `recovery_grid()` explains
the rest.

</details>

```{r convergence-tile, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Six tiles, one per design, with rows for 20 and 50 subjects and columns for 30, 100 and 300 trials. Each tile shows how many of its ten fits pass the convergence gate and which checks the others fail; the tiles at 30 trials are the lightest."}
plot_design(out, type = "convergence")
```

Every fit goes through bmmtools' convergence gate, which asks whether
the sampler explored the posterior well enough to trust the fit. A tile
counts the fits that fail each check, and one fit can fail more than
one.

<details>
<summary>What the gate checks</summary>

The gate checks every parameter of the fit, the between-subject
correlations and each person's values included. *R-hat* compares the
chains and should be close to 1; the gate allows at most 1.05. The
*effective sample size* (ESS) counts how many independent draws the
chains are worth, in the bulk and in the tails of the posterior; the
gate asks for at least 400. *Divergent transitions* are steps where the
sampler failed; the gate allows at most 10.

</details>

`r n_pass` of the `r nrow(cells)` fits pass; `r n_pass_101` pass if
R-hat must also be at most 1.01. Of the `r n_fail` fits that fail,
`r n_fail_30` are at 30 trials. In `r fail_on_cor` of the
`r n_fail`, the parameter whose ESS is lowest is one of the
between-subject correlations; in none is it a population mean. The
results below use every fit; using only those that pass changes no
`r_low` value (the lower end of the interval of r, defined with the
subject parameters) by more than `r fmt(r_low_shift, 3)`.

```{r cost, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Seconds per fit against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects; both rise with trials, and 50 subjects take longer at every number of trials."}
plot_design(out, metric = "fit_seconds")
```

A point is the mean seconds per fit of a design. Fitting took
`r fmt(res$minutes_fitting, 1)` minutes in all (bmm `r bmm_version`,
CmdStan `r res$toolchain[["cmdstan"]]`), between
`r fmt(min(cells$fit_seconds), 1)` and
`r fmt(max(cells$fit_seconds), 1)` seconds per fit.

<details>
<summary>The convergence numbers per design</summary>

```{r convergence-table, echo = FALSE}
by_design <- split(cells, ~ n_subjects + n_trials)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(by_design, function(d) {
  data.frame(
    subjects = d$n_subjects[[1]], trials = d$n_trials[[1]],
    `fits passing the gate` = sum(d$converged),
    `passing with R-hat ≤ 1.01` = sum(d$converged_101),
    `fits with any divergence (the gate allows 10)` =
      sum(d$n_divergent > 0),
    `mean seconds per fit` = fmt(mean(d$fit_seconds), 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(
  tab[order(tab$subjects, tab$trials), ],
  row.names = FALSE, align = "r"
)
```

</details>

## Population means

```{r population, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Bias, RMSE, coverage and credible interval width of the population means of drift, bound and ndt, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects."}
plot_design(out)
```

For each fit the estimate is the posterior median. *Bias* is the mean,
over the ten replications, of estimate minus generating value; *RMSE* is
the root of the mean squared difference; *CrI width* is the mean width
of the 95 % credible interval (CrI); all three are on the link scale.
*Coverage* is the share of the replications whose 95 % CrI contains the
generating value. Intervals of the right width contain it 95 % of the
time; intervals that contain it less often are too narrow, and ones that
contain it more often are too wide.

The population means are recovered without visible bias: at most
`r fmt(max(abs(pop$bias)), 3)` in absolute value. More subjects narrow
the intervals at every design and, for drift, lower the RMSE. Coverage
is where ten replications show their limit. The CrI of `bound` covered
in `r bound_k` of `r reps` replications with 50 subjects at both 30 and
100 trials. The Wilson interval of `r bound_k` of `r reps` runs from
`r interval(bound_k, reps)`, ending just below 0.95: weak evidence, at
two designs, that these intervals are too narrow. Pooled over all six
designs, `bound`'s intervals cover at a rate whose interval contains
0.95 (the pooled coverage figure below).

```{r pooled, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Coverage of the 50 % and 95 % intervals of each parameter, pooled over all designs, for population means and between-subject SDs, with 95 % Wilson intervals and a dashed line at the nominal rate. Population ndt sits above the nominal rate in both."}
plot_design(out, type = "coverage")
```

This figure pools the six designs, so each parameter has 60 intervals,
enough to see what one design cannot. Besides the 95 % interval, every
fit also reported a 50 % interval, a second check of the width: it
should contain the truth half of the time. Population means are in the
upper row, between-subject SDs in the lower. For every parameter and
level but one,
the Wilson interval of the pooled rate contains its nominal value, at
50 % and at 95 %. Population `ndt` is the exception: its 50 % intervals cover in
`r ndt_50` of `r nrow(ndt_rows)` (Wilson interval
`r interval(ndt_50, nrow(ndt_rows))`, which excludes 0.50) and its
95 % intervals in all `r ndt_95`. Its intervals are wider than their
nominal mass. This run is the only evidence for it so far: it has not
been checked on a second set of simulated data.

<details>
<summary>The population numbers per design</summary>

*Contraction* is 1 − (posterior SD / prior SD)²: near 1 when the data
determine the estimate and near 0 when the posterior is still the prior.
For `bound` and `ndt` it is at least
`r fmt(min(pop$contraction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`, a posterior SD at most
`r fmt(sd_ratio, 2)` times the prior SD. `drift` has none, because its
default prior on the population value is a Cauchy distribution, which
has no SD.

```{r population-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = pop$n_subjects, trials = pop$n_trials, parameter = pop$term,
  bias = fmt(pop$bias, 3), RMSE = fmt(pop$rmse, 3),
  covered = covered(pop$coverage),
  `CrI width` = fmt(pop$ci_width, 3),
  contraction = ifelse(
    is.na(pop$contraction), "–", fmt(pop$contraction, 3)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## Between-subject SDs

```{r sd, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Bias, RMSE, coverage and credible interval width of the between-subject SDs of drift, bound and ndt, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects."}
plot_design(out, level = "sd")
```

The SDs are read the same way, on the link scale. Their bias is at most
`r fmt(max(abs(sds$bias)), 3)`, for `r sd_worst$term` at
`r sd_worst$n_subjects` subjects and `r sd_worst$n_trials` trials. Their
coverage drops to `r covered(min(sd_300$coverage))` at 300 trials
(`r paste0(sd_low$term, " with ", sd_low$n_subjects, " subjects", collapse = ", ")`),
with the same wide Wilson interval as above; pooled over the designs,
every SD's interval contains the nominal rate (the figure above).

<details>
<summary>The SD numbers per design</summary>

```{r sd-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = sds$n_subjects, trials = sds$n_trials, parameter = sds$term,
  bias = fmt(sds$bias, 3), RMSE = fmt(sds$rmse, 3),
  covered = covered(sds$coverage), `CrI width` = fmt(sds$ci_width, 3),
  contraction = fmt(sds$contraction, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## Subject parameters

```{r subject, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "r, model-based reliability and coverage of the subject parameters of drift, bound and ndt, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects. drift has the lowest r and reliability at every design."}
plot_design(out, level = "subject")
```

Here each person's estimate is compared with that person's generating
value. The question is how well a study of this size ranks people, which
is what an analysis of individual differences needs.

- *r* is, within one replication, the correlation between estimated and
  generating values across the people. The ten values of r are averaged
  after Fisher's z transformation. Its bar runs from *r_low* to
  *r_high*, the usual 95 % interval of that average,
  `tanh(z ± 1.96 / sqrt(N))` with `N` the sum of (people − 3) over the
  replications. r_low is the value the section "How many trials?" uses,
  because it is r with the uncertainty of ten replications taken off.
- *Reliability (model)* answers the same question without the truth, so
  a study can compute it on its own data: `var(m) / (var(m) + mean(v))`,
  with `m` the posterior means of the people and `v` their posterior
  variances, per replication and then averaged. Its bars are too short
  to see.
- *Coverage* is the share of all people's 95 % CrIs that contain their
  generating value. It stays within
  `r fmt(max(abs(subj$coverage - 0.95)), 3)` of 0.95 at every design.

`bound` and `ndt` are recovered well from 30 trials on
(r ≥ `r fmt(min(subj$r[subj$term != "drift"]))`). `drift` is the hard
parameter: with 50 subjects its r is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 30, "drift")$r)` at 30 trials,
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r)` at 100 and
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r)` at 300. More people do not make
each person's estimate better: at no design does r differ by more than
`r fmt(max(abs(r_pair$at_20 - r_pair$at_50)), 3)` between 20 and 50
subjects. From 100 trials on, the reliability from the model differs
from the squared correlation with the truth (in the table below) by at
most `r fmt(max(abs(rel$reliability_gap[rel$n_trials >= 100])), 3)`, so
on real data of that size it says how well the people are ranked.

The two figures below show the first replication of the smallest and of
the largest design: each person's estimate against their generating
value, on the natural scale (seconds for `ndt`), with the 95 % CrI. The
dashed line is where estimate and truth are equal. These panels are in
alphabetical order.

```{r scatter-small, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Estimated against generating subject values for bound, drift and ndt with 20 subjects and 30 trials, one replication; the points scatter widely around the diagonal, most for drift."}
first <- out$level == "subject" & out$replication == 1
plot_recovery(out[first & out$condition == design_of(20, 30), ])
```

```{r scatter-large, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.8, fig.alt = "Estimated against generating subject values for bound, drift and ndt with 50 subjects and 300 trials, one replication; the points lie close to the diagonal with narrow intervals."}
first <- out$level == "subject" & out$replication == 1
plot_recovery(out[first & out$condition == design_of(50, 300), ])
```

<details>
<summary>The subject numbers per design</summary>

*Reliability from the truth* is the squared correlation of `m` with the
generating values; *gap* is the model's reliability minus it, per
replication, then averaged. Each is given with its MCSE, the SD over
replications divided by √10.

```{r subject-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = subj$n_subjects, trials = subj$n_trials, parameter = subj$term,
  r = fmt(subj$r), r_low = fmt(subj$r_low),
  `reliability from the truth` =
    with_mcse(rel$reliability_true, rel$reliability_true_mcse),
  `reliability from the model` =
    with_mcse(rel$reliability_model, rel$reliability_model_mcse),
  gap = with_mcse(rel$reliability_gap, rel$reliability_gap_mcse),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## The correlation between drift and boundary

```{r correlation, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Bias, coverage, credible interval width and the share of intervals excluding zero for the three between-subject correlations, against the number of trials, one line for 20 and one for 50 subjects. Only the drift-bound pair, generated at 0.4, has a share excluding zero well above zero."}
plot_design(out, level = "correlation")
```

The simulation drew each person's drift rate and boundary separation
from a population in which they correlate 0.4 and left the other two
pairs uncorrelated. A panel is named by the pair's two parameters:
`bound__drift` is the correlation between drift and boundary.
*Bias* is the mean estimate minus the generating value, 0.4 or 0.
*Share excluding 0* is the
share of replications whose 95 % CrI does not contain zero: for the 0.4
pair, the chance that a study of this size shows the correlation to
differ from zero (its power).

The CrIs of the 0.4 correlation contain it in nine or ten of the ten
replications at every design, but they are
`r fmt(min(target$ci_width))` to `r fmt(max(target$ci_width))` wide, so
they say little about its size. They exclude zero in at most
`r fmt(max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 50]), 1)` of the
replications with 50 subjects and
`r fmt(max(target$rejection_rate[target$n_subjects == 20]), 1)` with 20,
both at 300 trials: even then, a study with 50 people misses a
correlation of 0.4 between drift and boundary about one time in three.
With 20 subjects and 30 trials the estimate is pulled towards zero
(`r fmt(pick(target, 20, 30)$mean_estimate)` against an in-sample
`r fmt(pick(target, 20, 30)$in_sample)`, the mean correlation of the
values actually drawn; both are in the table below).

<details>
<summary>The correlation numbers per design</summary>

```{r correlation-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = cors$n_subjects, trials = cors$n_trials,
  pair = pair_label[cors$term], generating = fmt(cors$true_value, 1),
  `in sample` = fmt(cors$in_sample),
  `mean estimate` = fmt(cors$mean_estimate),
  covered = covered(cors$coverage),
  `CrI width` = fmt(cors$ci_width),
  `CrI excludes 0` = fmt(cors$rejection_rate, 1),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

</details>

## How many trials?

Take a threshold for r_low, 0.80 by default, a common convention for
measures used to rank individuals; 0.70 and 0.90 are given for readers
with another threshold. The answer is the smallest number of trials at
which r_low reaches the threshold for every parameter, and stays there
at every larger number of trials in the grid.

One more condition: at that design, the coverage of every population
mean must lie within one MCSE of 0.95, with the MCSE taken at 0.95,
`sqrt(0.95 × 0.05 / 10)` = `r fmt(res$coverage_mcse, 3)`. With ten
replications, 9 or 10 covered intervals out of 10 pass (0.90 is 0.05
from 0.95), and 8 fails (0.80 is 0.15 from it). A design at which the
population intervals are too narrow would be a poor recommendation,
however well it ranks people. `smallest_design()` applies this rule to
a grid summary:

```{r readoff-code, eval = FALSE}
s <- summary(out)
smallest_design(
  s[s$level %in% c("subject", "population"), ],
  c(r_low = 0.8),
  coverage_check = TRUE
)
```

It answers per parameter. The table below gives, for each number of
subjects and threshold, the largest answer over the three parameters,
the one that holds for every parameter. The column *using r* applies the
threshold to r instead of r_low, without the coverage condition. Where
it is smaller, either r meets the threshold but ten replications are too
few to be sure that it does, or the coverage condition moved the answer
up.

```{r readoff, echo = FALSE}
in_grid <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "not reached in this grid", x)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  subjects = readoff$n_subjects, bar = fmt(readoff$threshold, 2),
  `smallest number of trials` = in_grid(readoff$smallest_with_coverage),
  `using r` = in_grid(readoff$smallest_point),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "r")
```

With 50 subjects and bmm `r bmm_version`, a study needs
**`r smallest(50, 0.8)` trials** per person for an r_low of at least
0.80 on every parameter. The grid has nothing between its trial counts,
so "300" means more than 100 and at most 300. `drift` decides the r_low
part of each answer: at 100 trials its r_low is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 100, "drift")$r_low)`, at 300
`r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r_low)`. That is also why 0.90 is
not reached: drift's r of `r fmt(pick(subj, 50, 300, "drift")$r)` at
300 trials meets it (the 300 under *using r*), its r_low does not. The
0.80 answer is safe on
r_low but not on coverage: `bound` covered in
`r covered(pick(pop, 50, 300, "bound")$coverage)` replications at that
design, and one more miss would turn the answer into "not reached in
this grid".

The answer at 0.70 shows how much ten replications can decide. By r_low
alone it is `r smallest(50, 0.7, "smallest")` trials. But at that
design `bound` covered in
`r covered(pick(pop, 50, 100, "bound")$coverage)`, so the rule moves on
to `r smallest(50, 0.7)` trials. With one more covered interval the
answer would have been 100, and the second run of this script (see "The
run"), with different starting values, gave exactly that. Read it as
"100 or 300".

The number of subjects hardly matters for these answers: with 20
subjects they are `r smallest(20, 0.7)` trials at 0.70 and
`r smallest(20, 0.8)` at 0.80. More people narrow the interval of r and
of the population estimates; they do not measure each person better.
At the 0.80 threshold, r alone would say 100 trials with 20 subjects: drift's
r there is `r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 100, "drift")$r)`, but its r_low is
`r fmt(pick(subj, 20, 100, "drift")$r_low)`.

## Reproducing the study

[`vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R`](`r script_url`) runs
the grid and writes the results this page reads, to
`vignettes/articles/assets/recovery-ezdm.rds`. It needs bmm
`r bmm_version` or later, brms, cmdstanr and CmdStan, and a copy of the
bmmtools source. Run it from the package's root folder with
`Rscript vignettes/articles/precompute/recovery-ezdm.R`; it took
`r fmt(res$minutes, 0)` minutes for the run shown here, four chains in
parallel. The
fitted models go to `vignettes/articles/precompute/fits/`.
